## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)
*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*
None of the secondary literature passages in the present dossier directly discuss this discourse, citing instead homonymous texts such as the *Licchavikumārakasutta* (AN 5.58), the simile of boys and a crow in the *Sutta Nipāta* (Sn 270–271), or the lexical term *kumāraka* in Vinaya regulations.
The verse teaching of the sutta has significant parallels across early Buddhist literature. SuttaCentral records verse-level parallels in Sanskrit and Chinese collections corresponding to the *Karmavarga* of the *Udānavarga* (UV 9, UVS 9, and the Tibetan translation Uv Kg 9) and the Chinese translations T 212 (chapter 10) and T 213 (chapter 9) [SuttaCentral]. Automated text-reuse analysis by DharmaNexus confirms reuse within the Udāna literature itself, aligning the text with the Tibetan *Udānavargavivaraṇa* (D4100) [DharmaNexus]. Within the Pāli canon and paracanonical literature, the sutta is cited or referenced in the *Peṭakopadesa* (Pe 2) and *Nettippakaraṇa* (Ne 37) [SuttaCentral], which DharmaNexus corroborates through substantial textual matches with the *Sāsanapaṭṭhānadutiyabhūmi* (Pe 2, §§3.1–5.3) and the *Nettivibhāvinī* [DharmaNexus]. Furthermore, DharmaNexus records extensive shared phrasing with the *Daṇḍa Sutta* (Ud 2.3), as well as thematic and verse alignments with the *Puṇṇātherīgāthā* (Thig 12.1, §§3.1–5.3) and its commentary, alongside narrative formulas shared with Vinaya and Saṁyutta Nikāya texts [DharmaNexus].
*No discussion of this text was found in the reference-literature corpus; the overview relies on SuttaCentral and DharmaNexus data.*
